subject: Anthropology
title: Radiocarbon Dating
description: A quick, practical guide to Radiocarbon Dating.

hook.text: Every living thing absorbs carbon-14. When it dies, the clock starts ticking. We can read that clock.

buildup.text: Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of carbon-14 in organic materials to estimate when an organism died.

discovery.text: It works on wood, bone, shell, and charcoal up to about 50,000 years old — covering most of recent human history.

twist.text: It's not perfectly precise. Calibration curves are needed because atmospheric carbon-14 levels vary over centuries.

climax.text: Radiocarbon dating revolutionized archaeology by giving absolute dates to sites that had only relative timelines.

punchline.text: Dead atoms tell us when life ended.

quiz.question: What does radiocarbon dating measure?
options: Decay of carbon-14 in organic materials

details.summary: Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of carbon-14 in organic materials to determine their age, effective up to about 50,000 years. Developed by Willard Libby in 1949, it revolutionized archaeology by providing the first reliable absolute dating method.
details.whyItMatters: Radiocarbon dating transformed archaeology from relative chronology to absolute timelines. It allowed researchers to connect events across continents and build a reliable global timeline of human prehistory for the first time.
takeaways: Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14 decay in organic materials
It is effective up to approximately 50,000 years before present
The method revolutionized archaeology by enabling absolute dating

faq.question: What materials can be radiocarbon dated?
faq.answer: Any organic material that absorbed carbon while alive — wood, charcoal, bone, shell, seeds, textiles, and some soils. Stone, metal, and pottery cannot be directly radiocarbon dated, though associated organic materials found nearby can provide dates.

faq.question: How accurate is radiocarbon dating?
faq.answer: Modern accelerator mass spectrometry provides dates with uncertainties of about 20-100 years for materials up to 50,000 years old. Calibration against tree-ring chronologies corrects for variations in atmospheric carbon-14 and improves accuracy.
